2610.26957.title: On the Nature of the BeWD System Nova FQ Circinus

figures.caption: Figure 1: $\sim$12-year photometric light curves of FQ Cir obtained from ASAS-SN and OGLE (see section II for details). The 2022 nova outburst of FQ Cir is clearly visible at day $\sim$9800.

Figure 2: Lomb-Scargle periodogram for the combined, de-trended photometry of FQ Cir. Vertical black dashed lines indicate peaks well in excess of the 1% FAP level (blue horizontal dashed line) and are labeled with the corresponding period. Magenta lines correspond to alias frequencies of those significant peaks with P$>$10 d. The yellow line marks the TESS period found by S26.

Figure 3: Segment-wise search for modulation in detrended ASAS-SN and OGLE light curve. Left: detrended light curves (using same color scheme as in Fig. 1). 2610.26957.abstract: The classical nova FQ Cir  (Schaefer et al. 2026) has recently been shown to have a Be star donor, and has been identified as a High Mass Cataclysmic Variable (HMCV), with an orbital period of $\sim 2.04d$ (twice the 1.02d periodogram peak). Using the extensive OGLE optical archive, together with existing observations from ASAS-SN we instead find significant modulation between $\sim 50-60$~days and propose that the orbital period is likely closer to $\sim 62d$. We interpret the low amplitude 1.02 d modulation as a non-radial pulsation of the Be star. We also reassess the HMCV classification based on properties of known Be star-white dwarf systems.

2610.27112.title: Slowly Rotating Fully Convective Stars at $\lesssim$ 1 Gyr: Evidence from the Hyades and Praesepe

figures.caption:
Figure 1: The color–magnitude diagrams (CMDs) of Praesepe and the Hyades, colored by the membership probabilities reported by [30].
The left panel shows stars with publicly available period measurements [70, 69, 25, 12, 13, 15, 73, 71, 22, 47, 84, 886 for Praesepe and 179 for the Hyades;], while the colored points in the right panel represent cluster members for which we searched for rotation periods using Zubercal $r$-band light curves (428 for Praesepe and 761 for the Hyades).
The membership probability decreases toward lower masses, as the photometric and proper-motion measurements become increasingly uncertain due to the faintness of these stars.
This does not necessarily indicate that the lower-mass stars are non-members; rather, their fainter magnitudes make it more difficult to distinguish cluster members from field stars based on the available measurements.

Figure 2: Comparison between the literature rotation periods (see subsection II.1) and those recovered from ZTF for Praesepe (blue) and Hyades (orange).
Circle points and crosses indicate accepted and rejected ZTF periods, respectively.
Rejected periods correspond to stars that fail our period-quality criteria, including LS maximum power $<$0.1, LS maximum power-to-median power ratio $<$10, or periods consistent with known ground-based systematic signals (within 0.05 days of 0.5 days, within 0.1 days of 1 day, and within 0.5 days of 29.5 days).
Bold crosses highlight measurements identified as period aliases of the systematics determined from the spectral window function (0.33, 0.50, 1.00, 29.5, 363.67, and 444.48 days) following the relation described in Equation 1.
Aliases are identified by requiring the observed ZTF frequency, (1/$P_{\rm obs}$), to match the predicted alias frequency from the literature space-based period, (1/$P_{\rm true}$), within 10%.
The corresponding true periods are then recovered by applying the inverse alias relation.
After alias correction, the ZTF periods show agreement with the literature catalogs for 93.2% and 95.0% of Praesepe and Hyades stars, respectively.

Figure 5: Similar to Figure 2, but for stars without previously reported rotation periods.
Only stars with a ZTF maximum LS power $>0.1$ and a ratio of maximum to median LS power $>10$ are shown.
Thin crosses indicate stars whose TESS period measurements were rejected (see Figure 4).
After vetting for systematic periods (horizontal blue dashed lines) and correcting for the failure modes (blue dashed curves), we visually inspected each star’s light curve by eye.
We adopted 9 periods from TESS/K2 and excluded 6 ambiguous periods (shown as solid points).
This left us with 26 stars in Praesepe and 100 stars in the Hyades.
The empty circles indicate the subset of stars for which a K2 period is available or the maximum LS power from TESS exceeds 0.1.

Figure 6: Comparison of $v\sin i$ and rotation period for stars in Praesepe and Hyades.
Stars with rotation periods from the literature are shown as smaller dots, while stars with newly measured rotation periods are shown as circles with black outlines.
Points are colored by their $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ color.
Higher-mass hotter stars (smaller $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$) exhibit a tighter $v\sin i$–$P_{\rm rot}$ relation, while lower-mass stars show larger scatter, likely due to systematic inflation of $v\sin i$ measurements from inadequately modeled spectral lines.
Our newly measured rotation periods follow the same general trend as literature measurements for stars of similar $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$.
Stars with $P_{\rm rot}>35$ days have low $v\sin i$ values $<$ 10 km/s, consistent with the expected low projected rotational velocities of slowly rotating stars and the apparent $v\sin i$ detection floor.

Figure 7: Field contamination probability ($P_{\rm field}$) for the cluster members.
The probability that each star is a field contaminant, $P_{\rm field}$, is estimated using Gaussian mixture models of the cluster and field populations in astrometric and photometric parameter space.
Stars with available radial velocities are evaluated using 6D kinematics together with $G$ magnitude and $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$, while stars without radial velocities are evaluated using 5D astrometry and the same photometric quantities.
The resulting likelihoods are combined with the expected cluster and field fractions of the candidate sample using Equation 2.
Hyades and Praesepe members are shown in orange and blue, respectively, with the long-period stars ($P_{\rm rot}>35$ days) highlighted by larger symbols and colored according to their rotation periods.
The number of expected total number of field and cluster stars with similar 5D kinematics used to calculate the priors are shown on the top right corner.
5/10 stars in the Hyades and 0/5 stars in the Praesepe have $P_{\rm field}>0.01$.

Figure 8: Top: Normalized density of rotation period, $P_{\rm rot}$, as a function of absolute magnitude, $M_{G}$, in 0.5 mag bins.
Field stars are shown in gray, while the full Praesepe and Hyades samples, including periods newly identified in this work and periods from the literature [84], are shown in orange and blue, respectively.

In particular, the slowly rotating population persists with little change in the $M_{G}=10.5$–11 bin regardless of the membership-probability cut, suggesting that these stars are unlikely to be primarily field-star contaminants.
Bottom: Rotation-period distributions for stars with $P_{\rm rot}$$>35$ days in the cluster and field samples.
The cluster distribution does not closely match that of the field population, providing further evidence that the slow-rotating M dwarfs are not simply field-star contaminants.
We caution, however, that the sample sizes are small, with only 18 and 3 stars having $P_{\rm rot}$$>35$ days before and after applying the membership-probability cut, respectively, limiting our ability to robustly characterize the distribution of this population.

Figure 9: Fraction of stars with $P_{\rm rot}$$>35$ days as a function of effective temperature for the ZTF field sample, the full field sample combining rotation periods from all surveys as descirbed in subsection II.1, and the Hyades and Praesepe cluster samples.
The field samples are shown both with a 200 pc distance cut to better match the cluster sample.
All four samples exhibit a peak in the fraction of slow rotators, with the field samples peaking at $\sim 3500$ K and the Hyades and Praesepe peaking at $\sim 3300$ K.

The broader peak in the field samples may result from their wider metallicity distribution, while the narrower peaks in the clusters may reflect their more uniform metallicities.

2610.27112.abstract: We report the discovery of 10 stars in the Praesepe and Hyades clusters with unusually slow rotation that are likely not field contamination. Even though our search was general, all slow rotators are in the fully convective domain. We find that the fraction of slow rotators in the clusters is more than $5\sigma$ above the distribution expected from field contamination. They provide a potential link between the period distribution of the young open clusters and the field. These stars could be a distinct birth population, or they could be an indication that the onset of strong magnetic breaking is earlier than previously realized in this domain. Photometric variability and X-ray luminosity suggest the later but more data is needed to confirm. Searches for similar populations in younger clusters will help determine when slow rotators first emerge and constrain the timescale and physical mechanisms governing angular-momentum loss in fully convective stars. The discovery of these stars also highlights the importance of long-baseline photometric observations for detecting the long rotation periods of low-mass stars.

2610.27113.title: 20,000 Rotation Periods in Nearby Open Clusters and Moving Groups from ZTF and ASAS-SN

figures.caption:

The solid black line indicates the one-to-one relation, and the dashed black lines show the half-period harmonics.
Blue dashed lines indicate the alias relations predicted by Equation 1 based on the characteristic sampling periods.
Crosses mark sources identified as lying along these failure modes, for which I adopt the literature period.
Points show the accepted periods, colored by $-\log_{10}(\mathrm{FAP})$, with larger values indicating more statistically significant periodogram peaks.
After vetting and correcting the detected periods, 94% of the ZTF and 98% of the ASAS-SN measurements are consistent with the literature periods or their half- or double-period harmonics.

The new sample provides a more uniform coverage in age, increasing the number of clusters with age $<$100 Myr and $>$ 1 Gyr.
Some of these age regimes are particularly important for understanding rotational evolution where stars younger than $\sim$10 Myr can retain significant memory of their initial rotation conditions and stars at $\sim$20–100 Myr are expected to undergo substantial core–envelope decoupling for G dwarfs.

Figure 3: The period recovery fraction for the literature catalogs (left), the full rotation catalog from this work (middle), and the GOLD sample (right) in apparent Gaia $G$ magnitude–$G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ space.
The cutoffs at $G\sim 18$ and 12 mag indicate the faint and saturation limits for ZTF, respectively.
The recovery fraction is highest for K/M dwarfs, as expected given their typically higher photometric variability associated with their faster rotation.
The strips in the left panel reflect the small number of clusters with reported periods in the literature, whereas the full sample presented in this work provides more continuous coverage across $G$–$G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$ space as a substantially larger number of clusters are included.
In addition, the recovery fraction in [42] peaks at $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$$\sim$1 rather than among K/M dwarfs, highlighting the different sensitivities of the two instruments.

The left panel shows the measured rotation period, $\log_{10}(P_{\rm rot}/{\rm day})$, while the right panel shows the membership probability from Hunt and Reffert [33].
ZTF measurements are shown as colored circles and ASAS-SN measurements as gray outlined squares.
The EBs are excluded from this plot and the red points indicate the variable stars identified in the literature (see subsection II.4).
The full cluster membership sample is shown as light-gray points in the background.
The Gaia absolute $G$-band magnitudes are calculated using the cluster distances reported by Hunt and Reffert [33].

Figure 5: Main result of this work.
The top panel shows log${}_{10}P_{\rm rot}$ as a function of stellar absolute $G$-band magnitude, while the bottom panel shows the same rotation periods as a function of $G_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP}$.
The color scale indicates $\log_{10}(\mathrm{Age})$ on the top and photometric variability on the bottom.
The evolution from slow rotation during pre-main-sequence contraction to spin-down on the main sequence is visible across the diagram.
The EBs and variable stars are excluded from this plot, but most are distributed relatively uniformly across the hotter end of the temperature range.
The fastest rotators with $\log_{10}(P_{\rm rot}/{\rm day})<0.25$ are likely dominated by tidally synchronized binaries.
The bottom panel illustrates the decrease in variability toward longer rotation periods, also as expected.

Figure 6: Rotation–activity relation for cluster members in ZTF (left) and ASAS-SN (right).
Photometric variability, $R_{\rm var}$, is shown as a function of Rossby number, $Ro=P_{\rm rot}/\tau_{c}$, with points colored by cluster age.
Literature-identified EBs and variable stars are shown as cyan points and generally lie above the normal activity trend.
The light-gray points in the background in the right panel show the full ZTF cluster sample for comparison.
The gap near $\log_{10}Ro\sim-2.25$ results from the removal of periods associated with the 1-day systematic.
The approximately flat relation at Ro$<0.1$ corresponds to the saturated activity regime, while the decline in $R_{\rm var}$ toward larger Rossby numbers traces the unsaturated regime.
The youngest stars with enhanced variability near $\log_{10}$R$\sim-1.25$ and the relatively old, rapidly rotating stars with low variability around the same Ro are highlighted as distinct populations warranting further investigation.

2610.27113.abstract: Open clusters provide uniquely powerful laboratories for studying stellar evolution because their members share a common age and chemical composition. Stellar rotation of low-mass GKM dwarfs in open clusters provides direct empirical constraints on magnetic braking, with implications for stellar interiors, magnetic activity, and star--planet interactions. However, existing cluster rotation samples are dominated by space-based observations, whose limited spatial coverage and short observing baselines can make it difficult to construct an unbiased sample. Long-baseline ground-based time-domain surveys therefore provide an important complement to space-based photometry. I present a catalog of $\sim$20,000 periodic photometric signals, including stellar rotations, eclipsing-binaries, and classical pulsators, measured from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the All-Sky Automated Survey for Supernovae (ASAS-SN) for members of nearby open clusters and moving groups within 1.5 kpc. This catalog provides a new empirical foundation for studying the mass, chemical composition, and age dependence of stellar angular-momentum evolution and for testing models of magnetic braking across a broad range of stellar masses and evolutionary states.

2610.27186.title: Evolution of Massive Main-Sequence Stars in Binary Population Synthesis. II. Consequences for Black Hole High-Mass X-ray Binaries and Binary Black Holes

2610.27186.abstract: Interactions and mass loss during the main-sequence (MS) phase of massive binary stars can significantly alter their subsequent evolution and the properties of the black holes (BHs) they ultimately produce. We use the rapid binary population synthesis code \textsc{COMPAS}, incorporating a new treatment of MS evolution that self-consistently tracks the convective core under arbitrary mass-loss or mass-gain histories. We explore the properties of black hole high-mass X-ray binaries (BH-HMXBs) and binary black holes (BBHs) formed under this new framework. We find that a more detailed treatment of MS evolution is necessary to reproduce the high BH masses observed in BH-HMXBs, which are otherwise absent under prescriptions that do not take the internal structure of MS stars into account. Matching the observed rates and orbital periods favors case A mass transfer that is more non-conservative than commonly assumed. We further find that mass transfer of helium-enriched material during case A mass transfer is common in massive binaries, with potential consequences for the structure of the accreting star. For the BBH population, the new MS framework alters the chirp-mass and mass-ratio distributions of detectable mergers, and case A mass transfer can make a substantial contribution to the BBHs formed through the stable mass transfer channel. These systems show a strong preference for near-equal mass ratios, broadly consistent with recent constraints from gravitational-wave observations.

2610.28005.title: Phakoseismology: Asteroseismology of gravitationally microlensed stars

figures.caption: Figure 1: Microlensed oscillating source. The three coloured disks show the source star at different positions as its line of sight passes close to that of a lensing object. The gray dot shows the projected position of the lens, and the thin lines correspond to equal lens magnification strengths. Exaggerated bright and dark surface regions on the disks illustrate the local flux perturbations caused by stellar oscillations. As the lens and source approach each other in projection, the magnification varies across the stellar disk and weights different parts of the mode pattern unequally. Even when the disks overlap in projection, the source is not occulted. Light is deflected to angles of order the Einstein radius, far beyond the physical disk of the lens, so close approaches produce magnification rather than shadowing.

Figure 2: Geometry and coordinate systems. Left: Sky-plane geometry of a close microlensing event, with all angular separations scaled to the Einstein radius. The source is separated from the lens by $u$ and has angular radius $\rho_{s}$; the nearest approach occurs at $u_{0}$, and the surface is discretised into elements at separation $u^{\prime}$ from the lens. Middle: Orientation of the stellar rotation axis, $\mathbf{n}_{s}$. The coordinate system has $\hat{Z}$ pointing towards the observer, so the $\hat{X}$–$\hat{Y}$ plane defines the sky plane (shown transparent). The inclination ($i$) and azimuth ($\gamma$) define the three-dimensional orientation of the spin axis. Right: The two coordinate systems used in this work. The observer’s frame is shown as solid black curves at fixed polar angle $\theta$ and azimuth $\phi$; the stellar inertial frame is shown as dashed orange curves.

Figure 3: Illustrative noise-free oscillation power density spectra of a $1\,M_{\odot}$ star at three evolutionary stages. The spectra include modes up to $l=9$ and use the microlensing-modified mode visibilities calculated in this work. Mixed modes, instrumental noise, and effects from rotational splitting and granulation have been omitted. Columns from left to right show source-lens separations of $u/\rho_{s}=1000$, $1$, and $0.5$, while rows from top to bottom show the red giant, subgiant, and main-sequence stages.

Figure 4: Microlensing enhances the visibility of high-degree modes. Relative squared visibilities $V_{l}^{2}/V_{0}^{2}$ are shown for angular degrees $l=0$–$12$, coloured by the scaled source-lens separation $u$, which varies from $0$ (central transit) to $2\rho_{s}$. Note the orders-of-magnitude increase in visibility for high-$l$ modes as the lens approaches the stellar disk ($u\lesssim\rho_{s}$).

Figure 5: Azimuthal power distribution reveals the spin orientation. The colour map represents the relative distribution of power among azimuthal orders $|m|$ for a given multiplet $l$, plotted as a function of the spin-axis orientation, with inclination ($i$) on the vertical axis and azimuth ($\gamma$) on the horizontal axis. From left to right, the lens moves from a large separation ($u=1000\,\rho_{s}$) to a close transit ($u=0.5\,\rho_{s}$). At close separation, the distribution of power among the azimuthal orders depends on the angle $\gamma$, breaking the rotational degeneracy.

Figure 6: Recovery of the three-dimensional stellar spin axis. We present likelihood maps for the inclination ($i$) and sky-projected azimuth ($\gamma$) derived from the spectral power of multiplets $l=1,2,3$ (each displayed on a separate row) at three lens separations $u/\rho_{s}=1000,\,2,\,0.5$ (along each column). The input orientation $(i,\gamma)=(50^{\circ},70^{\circ})$ and the reference orientation $(i,\gamma)=(50^{\circ},0^{\circ})$ are shown in black and red, respectively. The spheres follow the format of Fig. 2 and indicate the stellar spin direction, while the colour map shows the posterior probability distribution given the input orientation. Individual modes or epochs leave extended allowed regions, while the combined likelihood (bottom panel) pinpoints the true orientation.

2610.28005.abstract: Asteroseismology relies on disk-integrated photometry or radial velocities, in which geometric cancellation suppresses modes of high spherical degree ($l\geq4$). Observations are thus limited to deeply penetrating, low-degree modes, leaving the outer envelope inaccessible. We investigate whether a high-magnification microlensing event can temporarily lift this limitation by differentially magnifying the surface of an oscillating source star. We modelled the visibility of solar-like oscillations during microlensing, weighting the surface by limb darkening and the local magnification. We computed multiplet visibilities and the power distribution among azimuthal components, and built a likelihood model for recovering the 3D spin-axis orientation from resolved rotational multiplets. When the lens-source separation becomes comparable to the source's angular radius, the magnification gradient acts as a transient spatial filter that breaks the symmetry of disk integration, raising high-degree mode visibilities by up to three orders of magnitude. The same non-axisymmetric weighting makes the relative power of azimuthal components depend on both the inclination and sky-projected azimuth of the spin axis, imprinting the full spin orientation onto the power spectrum. With $5\%$ relative-power uncertainties, we recover the orientation to $\sigma_i=2.9^\circ$ and $\sigma_\gamma=11.5^\circ$. Microlensing thus does more than amplify distant stars: its magnification pattern enables spatially selective asteroseismology. The effect is strongest for rare close encounters and unlikely to support large samples, and the newly visible high-degree modes will overlap with rotationally split and mixed modes, complicating mode identification. Nevertheless, individual high-quality events may open a window on envelope physics and spin geometries for stars in the Galactic bulge and beyond.

2610.28123.abstract: The Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS) and associated interplanetary sector boundaries fundamentally structure the solar wind environment, modulating coronal mass ejection (CME) evolution and solar energetic particle transport. In this study, we evaluate the capability of a static Potential Field Source Surface (PFSS; $R_{ss}=2.5R_\odot$) coronal model to directly map interplanetary sector boundary crossings from the Sun to 1 au without dynamic heliospheric propagation models. We compare ballistically transported HCS crossings derived from GONG-ADAPT and SDO/HMI magnetic maps against sector boundary crossing observations from the SBCross catalog. PFSS modeling reproduces the large-scale interplanetary magnetic field topology well ($J\approx0.50$), achieving hit rates (POD) of 0.64 for GONG-ADAPT and 0.76 for HMI. Carrington synoptic maps outperform flux-transport modeled maps, suggesting that the short-term observational noise from data assimilation degrades topological matching more than map "aging". Predictive skill shows a strong solar cycle dependence, performing significantly better during solar maxima (POD=0.70-0.81) than solar minima (POD=0.56-0.67), attributed to more distinct crossings due to higher HCS inclination angles during maximum. Matched events exhibit travel times close to ballistic estimates of 4.8-4.9 days with an average timing difference centered near zero ($\pm1.1$ days) and 90% of events within $\pm 1.8$ days. The hit rate of HCS structures that interact with CMEs does not degrade (POD = 0.67-0.83), despite propagating $\approx7$ hours faster on average, implying that the CME interaction causes only minor structural changes to the HCS. Larger timing differences (>24 hours) are associated with flatter current sheets. Overall, static PFSS extrapolations offer a computationally inexpensive, effective approach for mapping global sector boundary structure.

2610.28139.abstract: Heliospheric sector boundary crossings (SBCs), composed of the Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS), Heliospheric Plasma Sheet (HPS), and surrounding plasma halo, represent fundamental structures in the solar wind that influence interplanetary dynamics and space weather. We present the \textsc{SBCross} catalog, an automated, publicly available database containing 1,076 SBC events derived from in-situ observations spanning more than 30 years (1995--2026), covering Solar Cycles 23 and 24 alongside the rising and maximum phases of Solar Cycle 25. By combining interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) and 255~eV suprathermal electron pitch angle distributions (PAD) data, our algorithm reliably captures large-scale polarity transitions, with $76\%$ of detected SBCs exhibiting clear HPS signatures ($\beta > 1$, $n_{\mathrm{peak}} > 10\mathrm{\,cm^{-3}}$). Across the catalog, we find an average occurrence rate of $\approx 2.6$ events per Carrington rotation, a median event duration of $\approx 9.0$\,hours, and a median physical thickness of $\approx 7.4 \times 10^6$\,km. Furthermore, approximately $\approx 15\%$ of detected SBCs interact with interplanetary coronal mass ejections (CMEs) on average, with this proportion rising up to $33\%$ during solar maximum. These CME-associated events exhibit systematically longer durations (median of $10.0$\,hours), $54\%$ larger physical thicknesses, and higher average solar wind velocities. Notably, all high-velocity SBC events ($> 600\mathrm{\,km\,s^{-1}}$) are exclusively driven by CME interactions, demonstrating local plasma pile-up and structural entanglement resulting from fast CMEs overtaking the ambient slow background. The \textsc{SBCross} catalog serves as an updated successor to the classic SBC list by L. Svalgaard, delivering a standardized, open-access resource for the heliophysics community to systematically investigate sector boundary transitions.

2610.28220.abstract: We use a Monte Carlo analysis to study whether wide binaries can be represented by bound Newtonian orbits, and, if this is the case, whether the distribution of the orbital parameters agrees with expectations. The potential orbits are classified according to the $\chi^2$ probability of representing star coordinates, parallaxes, velocity components and masses. We apply this analysis to 44 systems previously published, to which we add 26 wide binaries, consisting of twin low-mass (M) stars. We find orbital solutions for 65 systems, and derive the distribution of their orbital parameters. For one system composed of M-type stars, no Newtonian bound solution can be found; however, this pair is a member of the young Argus association and therefore not a suitable target. The remaining four systems that cannot be fit were already identified as likely disrupted binaries. The uncertainty in the separation between the components, given by the parallax error, is by far the dominant error source, and the main limitation of the present analysis, affecting especially the determination of the orbits' inclination angle and phase. Newtonian dynamics describe well our sample. When dividing the sample into two subsamples, according to the mutual acceleration, the eccentricity and periastron distributions agree with theoretical expectations; inclination and phase are distorted by the parallax-limited separation, more strongly in the high-acceleration (37 systems) than in the low-acceleration ($A_N < 10^{-9} m s^{-2}$, 28 systems) subsample, which is opposite to what a gravitational signal would produce. In particular the ratio between observed velocity difference and circular velocity does not show any excess for the low acceleration sample. When parametrized as a boost $\gamma$ parameter to the velocity, $0.95 < \gamma <1.05 (1 \sigma)$, fully consistent with Newton also for the low acceleration sample.

2610.28274.abstract: (Abridged abstract): A key component of the widely used Wang-Sheeley-Arge model is the tracing of magnetic field lines in the solar corona, as that largely determines the modeled open/closed field regions and in turn the predicted large-scale solar wind structure. We demonstrate that by slightly raising the height from which magnetic field lines are traced from the photosphere (R$_{su}$), we can improve the prediction of solar wind high-speed enhancements (HSEs). We find a higher R$_{su}$ produces more accurate estimates of the HSE start time, duration, and peak speed, and enables the detection of HSEs that were missed with the standard R$_{su}$. These improvements are primarily associated with changes in the great-circle angular distance, while the flux tube expansion factors remain largely unchanged. A higher R$_{su}$ produces smoother open-field boundaries and reduces small-scale fragmentation within open-field regions. These morphological changes lead to more stable magnetic footpoint mappings and consequently more robust GCD calculations. To assess the statistical relevance of these findings, we extend the analysis to 53 Carrington rotations and perform a multi-metric evaluation of model performance. The results indicate that higher R$_{su}$ improves HSE predictions while reducing false alarms. We thus find that the choice of R$_{su}$ represents an important and previously underexplored parameter that can help enhance our ambient solar wind modeling and forecasting capabilities.

2610.28292.abstract: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events, operationally defined as proton flux exceeding 10 pfu in the >10 MeV channel, threaten spacecraft systems, astronaut safety, and high latitude aviation, yet continuous real-time forecasting with adequate lead time remains difficult. We present SEPNET-PRISM-R, a near-real-time system that issues hourly, 24 hour ahead probabilistic SEP forecasts. The model integrates multimodal solar data - including active region patches, flare features, coronal mass ejection (CME) characteristics, and historical proton flux - to concurrently predict SEP occurrences, peak proton flux, soft X-ray flux, and CME velocity, with the primary objective being SEP forecasting. Building on existing literature, SEPNET-PRISM-R enhances operational performance by incorporating a postprocessing module that enables cross-validated decision making and interpretable quantification of feature importance. The training dataset spans from February 1986 to September 2025, with subsequent forecasts generated sequentially through the present via a real-time space weather prediction platform that provides predictive probabilities, feature attributions, and historical analogs, enabling more reliable and informed operational decision-making. The proposed framework substantially suppresses false alarm rates while maintaining robust event detection capabilities, as evidenced by case studies and aggregate statistics.

2610.28331.abstract: Massive protostellar disks are expected to sustain high accretion rates through gravitational instability, while dust growth may modify their opacity, cooling efficiency, and stability. Conversely, the time-dependent and nonaxisymmetric structures produced by gravitational instability may regulate the local conditions for dust growth. However, the coupled evolution of dust growth and gravitational instability in massive protostellar disks has not yet been explored self-consistently. We present two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations that follow gas dynamics, dust growth, and opacity-dependent radiative cooling in a massive protostellar disk. We find that dust grains rapidly grow to millimeter-centimeter sizes shortly after disk formation, substantially reducing the infrared opacity. The enhanced cooling promotes disk fragmentation and produces more frequent accretion-driven luminosity outbursts than in a model without dust growth, with durations and peak luminosities comparable to those observed in massive protostars. Dust growth is broadly regulated by the fragmentation-limited size in dense disk regions, whereas newly formed outer disk regions and low-density regions deviate from this limit because of finite collision timescales and dust transport. These results suggest that dust growth may facilitate episodic accretion and fragmentation, while gravitationally unstable disk structures in turn regulate the dust growth process.

2610.28345.abstract: Age is the one of the most difficult stellar properties to constrain. However, upcoming surveys such as PLATO are about to revolutionize our ability to measure FGK dwarf ages with asteroseismology. Here, we use The Cannon to construct a data-driven model for inferring asteroseismic-quality age measurements from large spectroscopic survey observations and demonstrate that forthcoming asteroseismology datasets from future surveys can be leveraged, together with our model, to obtain stellar age samples larger than can be obtained by those surveys alone. We train The Cannon on 323 FGK dwarf stars with asteroseismic age labels from NASA Kepler photometry and high-resolution spectra from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE). We apply our model to FGK dwarfs from the Kepler survey that exhibit solar-like oscillations and reproduce their reported asteroseismic-quality ages with an RMS scatter of 1.0 Gyr. We then apply our model to the sample of 3810 Kepler FGK dwarfs with APOGEE spectra to infer data-driven asteroseismic ages. We repeat this for the larger sample of 48,828 FGK dwarfs with APOGEE spectra. Our work demonstrates that data-driven methods can robustly reproduce asteroseismic ages for FGK dwarfs. These methods will be invaluable tools for extending asteroseimology measurements from upcoming surveys (e.g., PLATO) to much larger stellar samples.

2610.28352.abstract: Blue supergiants (BSGs) are crucial to understanding the evolution of massive stars. Although distinguishing between pre- and post-red supergiant (RSG) phases is challenging, stellar pulsations provide valuable constraints on their masses and evolutionary status. This study analyzes TESS light curves of six BSGs with high L/M to identify periodicities. We performed theoretical modeling of the radial unstable modes to characterize the strange modes. We aim to estimate asteroseismic masses, compare them with spectroscopic and evolutionary mass estimates, and assess the evolutionary stage of the stars. We employed the Lomb-Scargle periodogram and the weighted wavelet Z-transform to address quasiperiodic behavior and time-varying signals. A linear nonadiabatic stability analysis was performed to test for radial perturbations, generating eigenfrequencies that enable stellar mass estimation. In addition, we characterized the stochastic low-frequency variability (SLFV). We derive a first guess at the asteroseismic masses. We find that HD 74371 and HD 79186 are evolving blueward following the RSG phase, while the evolutionary stage of HD 115842 cannot be uniquely determined with the available mass estimates. We also find that HD 52382 and HD 99953 are likely in the post-RSG phase; however, their low masses are difficult to reconcile with the available evolutionary models. The extreme supergiant HD 80077 shows the largest mass discrepancy in the sample, suggesting a more complex evolutionary history. The SLFV properties do not provide a clear diagnostic of the evolutionary stage. These results highlight the potential of asteroseismology as a complementary tool for constraining the evolutionary status of BSGs. However, the mass discrepancies found for some objects indicate that additional observational and theoretical efforts are required.

2610.28443.abstract: The apparent absence of magnetism in subdwarf B stars (sdBs) has emerged as an outstanding observational puzzle, especially in light of their likely origin in binary interactions. Gravity-mode pulsations in some sdBs offer a unique opportunity to extend recent successes in asteroseismic magnetic field detection in red giants. In the presence of strong magnetic fields, gravity modes are expected to be significantly damped, suppressing their observed amplitudes. We place stringent upper limits on magnetic fields in 30 hot subdwarfs by using the observation of low-frequency dipole and quadrupole modes to rule out magnetic suppression. Even under conservative assumptions, our upper limits constrain near-surface magnetic fields to below a kilogauss in roughly half of our sample, with the strongest individual constraint reaching down to $\sim20\,\mathrm{G}$. These upper limits reinforce the apparent dearth of magnetic fields in hot subdwarfs and demonstrate asteroseismology as a powerful new probe of magnetism in these stars.

2610.28513.abstract:
Resonant three-mode coupling is a fundamental nonlinear process in stellar oscillations and other wave systems. We investigate the global dynamics of a linearly overstable parent mode coupled to two damped daughter modes. The principal control parameters are frequency detuning $\Delta$ and daughter damping rate $\Gamma$, normalized by the parent growth rate. We combine high-resolution maps of the largest Lyapunov exponent in the $(\Gamma,\Delta)$ plane with linear stability analysis, Floquet calculations, and numerical continuation. The resulting parameter space includes stable equilibria, simple and period-doubled limit cycles, chaotic attractors, formally unbounded solutions, and higher-period `shrimp' islands within chaotic regions. Successive period doublings lead to chaos, while boundaries of isolated periodic windows exhibit type-I intermittency.
At large $\Gamma$, the main bifurcation boundaries approach straight lines, indicating that the dynamics is governed primarily by $r=\Delta/(2\Gamma)$. We connect finite-$\Gamma$ bifurcations to an earlier one-dimensional return map. As $\epsilon\rightarrow0$, this map recovers the principal period-doubling sequence, the onset of chaos near $r\simeq0.38$, and the asymptotic positions of prominent periodic windows. We also examine the effects of unequal daughter damping rates.
Applying these results to sporadic outbursts in cool DAV white dwarfs, we find that estimated $g$-mode growth rates, damping rates, and detunings place resonant triplets in both periodic and chaotic regimes. Thus, instability of the three-mode equilibrium need not produce a regular limit cycle: deterministic chaos and intermittency may contribute to irregular outburst amplitudes and recurrence times.

2610.28603.abstract: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events threaten space infrastructure, yet physics-based prediction models depend on numerous poorly constrained free parameters. We introduce the Fujitsu Solar Energetic particle Intelligent Tuning and Evaluation Network (SEITEN), which couples the SUSANOO MHD model of CME propagation to SEPIF, a diffusive shock acceleration and focused transport model, through the shock conditions SUSANOO supplies, and automatically optimizes the free parameters of the particle model against the SEP event of 9 October 2021. The mean free path and the injection efficiency vary independently along each magnetic field line and heliolongitudinal bin, giving a 19-dimensional problem solved by quasi-Monte Carlo sampling followed by a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. The optimized model reproduces proton flux profiles at five spacecraft with a mean absolute error of $\approx 0.45$ in $\log_{10}$ flux, and the inferred mean free paths show a clear east-west structure; these are effective parameters conditional on the assumed transport geometry. Six independent runs show that whether mean free paths or injection efficiencies dominate depends on the MHD shock strength, and that injection efficiencies differ by orders of magnitude between MHD configurations despite nearly identical fit quality. Joint MHD-SEP parameter estimation is therefore a necessary next step towards generalized, operational SEP forecasting.

2610.27055.abstract: The discovery of exoplanets around white dwarfs uniquely informs our understanding of planetary survival through stellar evolution. Common Envelope (CE) evolution is one of the proposed mechanisms that could shape the orbital architecture of these planets around stellar remnants. In this work, we predict the occurrence rate and orbital separation/planet mass distributions for planets that could form around white dwarfs through CE evolution. We simulate populations of giant-planet systems, sampling initial conditions from observed mass and semi-major axis distributions for main sequence stars. We evolve the host star from main sequence to white dwarf to assess which planetary configurations could survive, and we predict the resulting post-CE planet population. Our results suggest that such planets should be rare, massive, and have very close orbital separations. We find that most of the surviving planets have masses of $>10\,M_{\rm{Jup}}$ and orbital separations $<1.4$ times the tidal disruption radius, $a_{disrupt}$ ($\lesssim0.006$ AU, also called the Roche limit), which is in contrast to high eccentricity migration, which produces planets with orbital separations $>2a_{disrupt}$. The properties of CE survivors from our simulations contrast with the known closely-orbiting planet WD 1856+534 b, suggesting a different mechanism may be responsible for its formation.

2610.27081.abstract: The Einstein Telescope (ET), the European next-generation gravitational-wave observatory, is at a decisive stage: the choice of its detector configuration is still open, with profound implications for its scientific output. We provide a quantitative basis for this choice by comparing two candidate configurations at their proposed sites: the triangular design ($\Delta$) at the Euregio Meuse-Rhine site, and the 2L design, with interferometers in Sardinia, Italy, and Lusatia, Germany. We present the first realistic estimates of sky-localization uncertainties for binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, moving beyond Fisher-matrix forecasts to full Bayesian parameter estimation that captures the multimodal structure of the sky posterior. We focus mainly on the high-frequency interferometers alone, providing an expected scenario for the first years of ET operations, as the more challenging low-frequency instruments will come online later. BNS injections span different sky positions and luminosity distances between 40 and 2000 Mpc, corresponding to signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) from 12 to 720. Our analysis relaxes the long-wavelength approximation and includes Earth's rotation and higher-order modes, all of which improve sky localization. We find that the $\Delta$ configuration localizes low- and moderate-SNR sources in eight degenerate sky modes spread across both hemispheres and over the day and night sides of the Earth, with 90% credible areas reaching $\sim 2 \times 10^4 \, \mathrm{deg}^2$. In contrast, the 2L configuration recovers a single dominant mode that contains at least 50% of the posterior probability and is one to two orders of magnitude smaller in area. This represents a substantial advantage for multimessenger follow-up campaigns.

2610.27183.abstract: Shock breakout is the first electromagnetic signal of a supernova, generating a highly luminous and fast-timescale burst of thermal radiation. Motivated by recent theoretical progress in producing successful three-dimensional supernova explosions of massive stars, we undertake a detailed numerical study on the impact that the core-collapse asymmetries might have on the breakout signal. We perform the first fully 3D multi-group radiation hydrodynamics simulations of shock breakout for the case of a red supergiant explosion. We find that large-scale asymmetries formed during the core-collapse process can extend the breakout flash duration to days, with the timescale set by the supernova shock fully wrapping around the progenitor star. Using detailed 3D radiative transfer post-processing, we generate synthetic multi-wavelength light curves and spectra to more closely connect to observations. The light curves show a significant viewing-angle dependence of the overall shape and peak brightness of shock breakout. We find that core-collapse asymmetries have the largest impact on the breakout light curve when observed in shorter UV wavelengths. On the other hand, at optical wavelengths, we find a diminished impact of the asymmetric breakout that more closely resembles a 1D spherical breakout. Our results show how multi-dimensional effects originating from the core-collapse mechanism can play a major role in setting the shock breakout properties, and are particularly relevant to upcoming UV space missions such as ULTRASAT and UVEX.

2610.27252.abstract: The selection of candidates belonging to rare or underrepresented stellar populations, as well as novel objects, is essential for spectroscopic follow-up. In this work, we demonstrate how combining broad- and narrow-band photometric information with machine-learning techniques enables this selection. Using photometric data in twelve filters from the Javalambre Photometric Local Universe Survey (J-PLUS) as input, we applied an anomaly detection technique based on autoencoders to identify spectral energy distributions (SEDs) that deviate from the dominant pattern in the J-PLUS objects sample. Subsequently, we applied the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) algorithm to the J-PLUS colors of the outlier SEDs population. Combining information from the SIMBAD database and other astronomical surveys to classify the outliers identified by the autoencoder, we are able to characterize over-densities in the t-SNE map. Our study specifically focuses on well-defined islands in the t-SNE space, corresponding to specific populations. We identified a large sample of white dwarfs and low-mass stars, including a small subset of polluted white dwarfs, and report potential candidates for spectroscopic follow-up, including 19 carbon-rich stars, 11 cataclysmic variables and 170 white-dwarfs-main-sequence binaries, all previously unreported in the literature.

2610.27312.abstract: Supernova (SN) 1987A showed that some hydrogen-rich core-collapse supernovae (SNe) rise slowly to peak, defining a distinct subclass. Wide-field surveys have uncovered more extreme members, such as OGLE-2014-SN-73, SN 2020faa, and SN 2023vbw, that challenge neutrino-driven explosion models. We present ultraviolet-to-infrared, radio, X-ray, and spectropolarimetric observations of SN 2023iop at $z = 0.1020$, the most extreme 87A-like event to date. It rose for $\gtrsim88$ rest-frame days to $M_r \approx -20.1$ mag, also placing it among the hydrogen-rich superluminous SNe, and radiated $\gtrsim4\times10^{50}$ erg. Its spectra resemble those of typical Type II SNe and remain photospheric at $\sim330$ days post-maximum. Continuum polarization of 0.8-1.0% indicates an aspherical system. Hydrogen-rich pair-instability supernova (PISN) models of a $190~M_\odot$ star reproduce the light-curve up to 150 days after peak, but not the late-time emission. A late-time spectrum shows a feature near 7300 Å, tentatively identified as [Ni II] $\lambda$7378. The implied $\approx0.02~M_\odot$ of stable $^{58}$Ni is reached only in the most massive PISN models. The low-mass host galaxy ($\sim10^{8.2}~M_\odot$) is consistent with a metal-poor progenitor as required by the PISN channel. Fallback accretion reproduces the light-curve morphology, but not the colors. We consider a pair-instability explosion the most plausible scenario, with the late-time light-curve excess powered by circumstellar interaction, which shows no signatures in the spectra. SN 2023iop shows that the most luminous 87A-like events occupy an underexplored region of massive-star evolution.

2610.27484.abstract: The survival of exomoons around close-in white dwarf planets offers a potential constraint on their migration histories and an alternative pathway to post-main-sequence habitability. We investigate whether moons can survive the tidal circularization of planets via high-eccentricity migration, and consider a hierarchical three-body system (white dwarf-planet-moon) after an initial eccentricity excitation of the planetary orbit. Using an analytic equilibrium tidal model, we compare the evolution of the planetary and satellite orbits and examine the conditions required for an evection resonance. We show that the moons of pseudosynchronously rotating planets always migrate inwards since the planetary corotation radius always exceeds the Hill radius, independent of mass and orbital eccentricities. Comparing the migration timescales for the moon and the planet shows that compact moons undergo rapid tidal decay relative to the outer orbit. However, the wider separations favored by slower migration timescales experience pericenter perturbations whose work constitutes a substantial fraction of the moon's orbital energy. Together, our results indicate that moons likely do not survive during a planet's high-eccentricity migration phase in a three-body configuration.

2610.27807.abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) observations of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) exhibit significant diversity, but their physical origin remains poorly understood. We investigate UV spectra of SNe Ia observed with the Swift UltraViolet and Optical Telescope. Our expanded pre-maximum sample probes dependencies on decline rate, ejecta properties, and host environment. We recover the correlation between UV flux and decline rate near maximum in the near-UV (NUV), and find correlations at pre-maximum phases in both the NUV and mid-UV (MUV). This trend is strongly wavelength dependent, with slow decliners showing higher NUV but lower MUV flux than fast decliners. Synthetic TARDIS spectra varying the 56Ni abundance show that enhanced 56Ni suppresses the MUV while increasing the NUV, broadly reproducing the trend. We find no significant correlation between UV flux and ejecta velocity, while Si II 6355 pEW shows trends similar to those with decline rate. We also find no significant correlations with host-galaxy properties, although host environment may contribute to the remaining UV diversity among SNe with similar decline rates. Early-excess SNe show enhanced flux mainly in the NUV rather than a broad UV excess, suggesting that strong circumstellar interaction is not necessarily required to explain the observed excess emission. Peculiar subclasses show distinct UV properties, with brighter and hotter subclasses showing higher UV flux, although the current sample is small and does not cover all SN Ia subtypes. Our results suggest that the UV diversity of SNe Ia is shaped by multiple mechanisms that contribute differently across the UV wavelength range.

2610.27931.abstract: Characterisation of progenitor stars of supernovae (SNe) poses several challenges. Direct observations of progenitors are based on serendipitious archival observations and are only possible for nearby events. Indirect methods include inferring nickel mass from the light curves or oxygen masses from the SN's nebular phase, both of which are tools to constrain the progenitor's initial mass. Alternatively, environments of SNe have been used as a proxy for the progenitor's age and metallicity. The progenitor channel of type Ibn SNe is a hotly debated topic. The mass-loss and the formation of He-rich circumstellar medium requires strong envelope stripping of the progenitor star. For core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), this requires strong stellar wind mass losses, i.e. a Wolf-Rayet (WR) star, or binary interaction with a companion star. Here, we analyse a sample of host galaxies of type Ibn SNe that have been observed with MUSE. We use H$\alpha$ emission to infer the transient's association to star formation and derive the local metallicity with commonly used strong line diagnostic. We find that the sample of SNe are highly associated with star formation in the host galaxy, typically situated within one of the brightest HII regions in the host galaxy. The NCR distribution of H$\alpha$ pixels in SN Ibn environments strongly resembles that of WR stars, and shows a stronger preference to SF compared to other core-collapse SN types. Metallicity measurements show typically sub-solar metallicity in the SN environments.

2610.27949.abstract: The presence of HNCO in the gaseous phase is well known for the interstellar medium, but the molecule is not detected yet in the solid phase. We report the first laboratory-confirmed identification of solid HNCO at 2260 cm$^{-1}$ in open JWST data using laboratory infrared spectra. For that, we grew binary mixtures of HNCO with main constituents of interstellar ice using ISEAge setup at 10 K: HNCO:H$_2$O = 1:10, HNCO:CO = 1:10, HNCO:CO$_2$ = 1:10, HNCO:CH$_3$OH~=~1:10. We present transmission infrared spectra of pure HNCO and HNCO-bearing ices along with the corresponding band strengths at 10 K. The fitting of open JWST observational data with the laboratory reference spectra in a 10--23 K temperature range show that solid HNCO is predominantly located in the apolar layer rich in CO. The abundance of solid HNCO is approximately estimated as 0.04--0.15\% relative to solid H$_2$O. The positive correlation between HNCO and N$_2$O suggests their co-formation via the chemical route that includes solid N$_2$. The results are also supported by the numerical modeling of HNCO formation in protostellar objects with predicted abundance of 0.06--0.11\%. We calculated the upper limits for CH$_3$CN toward two protostars and evaluated its abundance to solid water using the spectroscopic fitting and modeling.

2610.28049.abstract: Context: Superbursts are energetic explosions in the crusts of neutron stars in Low-Mass X-ray Binaries (LMXBs). At temperatures above 4 GK, photodisintegration of heavy rp-process ashes may play a major role alongside $^{12}$C fusion. Aims: We investigate how photodisintegration of rp-process ashes affects superburst properties and the initial $^{12}$C abundance required for ignition. Methods: We simulate superbursts with MESA v.24.08.1. Besides the canonical fuel of $20\%$ $^{12}$C and $80\%$ $^{56}$Fe, we test different $^{12}$C abundances mixed with scaled rp-process ashes. Results: Superbursts can ignite with only $10\%$ $^{12}$C when the remaining $90\%$ consists of rp-process ashes. Their luminosity is comparable to that of the canonical fuel, whereas $10\%$ $^{12}$C mixed with $90\%$ $^{56}$Fe yields lower luminosity. $^{56}$Fe remains the most abundant ash nuclide. Although photodisintegration drives nucleosynthesis, neutron, proton and alpha captures release energy at late times. We also find that $A=64$ nuclides or $^{20}$Ne help reduce the $^{12}$C abundance needed for ignition. Conclusions: The composition of accreted material - not just its $^{12}$C content - substantially affects superburst ignition, luminosity and nucleosynthesis.

2610.28424.title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence

figures.caption: Figure 1: Evolution of turbulent cross helicity and mean magnetic field. The vertical axis shows the absolute value of each curve. Phase 1: KHI grows; the fastest growing mode is shown. Phase 2: KHI saturates and becomes fully 3D hydrodynamically (negligible Lorentz force at this stage). This alters the cross-helicity evolution. Phase 3: CHSI dominates; $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{b}\rangle_{V}$ and the mean magnetic field grow with the same exponential rate. Phase 4: saturation occurs when cross-helicity production balances losses. Parameters used are $u/(U_{0}a)=0.0125$ and $\eta/(U_{0}a)=0.02$. The spatial resolution is $512\times 512\times 1024$.

Figure 2: Mean-field profiles in the KHI phase (a) and the slowly growing CHSI phase (b). In the KHI phase, $B_{x}(z)$ is localized near the shear layer and can depend on initial perturbations. In the slow-growth CHSI phase, $B_{x}(z)$ follows the imposed $U_{x}(z)$, as predicted by Eq. (4) when $\lambda/(\beta_{T}k^{2})\ll 1$. The profiles are time-averaged and separately normalized for comparison. Since $B_{x}$ in the CHSI phase can change sign, that sign is taken into account while time-averaging. The simulation uses $\eta/(U_{0}a)=0.03$ and zero initial mean magnetic field.

Figure 3: Temporal analysis of sources and sinks in the turbulent cross-helicity budget (3). Since magnetic fields grow exponentially in the kinematic phase, each term of Eq. (3) is divided by the magnetic rms amplitude $b_{\rm rms}(t)$ and time-integrated, $[Q]=\int_{0}^{t}dt^{\prime}\,Q(t^{\prime})/b_{\rm rms}(t^{\prime})$, to assess the cumulative generation or loss of turbulent cross helicity via different mechanisms. The CHSI phase begins at $t\mathrm{\approx}200$. The turbulent cross helicity $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{b}\rangle_{V}$ is generated by the stress-production effect, in particular $\langle B_{x}T_{x}\rangle_{V}$. Since the source is generally larger than the sinks, the value of the black curve, though small, is almost always positive. This positive value provides the growth of $\langle\bf u\cdot\bf b\rangle_{V}$ observed in Fig. 1.

Figure 4: Spatial turbulent-cross-helicity budget during the kinematic CHSI phase. Turbulent cross helicity is produced in the shear layer by the Reynolds–Maxwell stress, while EMF transfer and visco-resistive dissipation act as losses; transport redistributes cross helicity without changing its volume average. Curves are time-averaged after normalizing them by $b_{\rm rms}$. Faint curves in the background show unfiltered data whereas the filtered data are shown with thick curves.

Figure 5: Physical interpretation of the cross-helical shear instability.
(a) In hydrodynamic shear turbulence, vertical turbulent motions $u_{z}$ advect the mean horizontal momentum $U_{x}$, producing fluctuations $u_{x}$. Turbulent kinetic energy grows via $P_{K}=\langle-R_{xz}\partial_{z}U_{x}\rangle_{V}$.
(b) In MHD, the same vertical motions advect the turbulence-generated mean magnetic field $B_{x}$, producing fluctuations $b_{x}$ aligned with $u_{x}$. Turbulent cross helicity grows via the stress production term $P_{W}=\langle-R_{xz}\partial_{z}B_{x}\rangle_{V}$. While $u_{x}$ and $b_{x}$ change sign along $x$ (or $y$ or both), the correlation $u_{x}b_{x}$ carries the same sign, making $W\mathrm{=}\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{b}\rangle_{V}$ non-zero and growing.
(c) CHSI feedback loop: a seed turbulent cross helicity $W$ generates $B_{x}$ through the cross-helicity EMF $\mathcal{E}_{y}\propto W$; the resulting mean field $B_{x}$ then enters the stress production $P_{W}\propto\partial_{z}B_{x}$, which acts as a source for $W$; and $W$ grows when its production exceeds losses. The CHSI does not require an initial mean magnetic field.

Figure S1: The KHI of the maintained shear flow drives turbulence that operates in the finite-shear regime, $S\sim\mathcal{O}(10)$. During the initial transient phase (up to $t\approx 200a/U_{0}$), flow fluctuations grow exponentially via KHI and become nonlinearly re-organized into saturated 3D structure. At this stage, the rate of energy injection ($k/\tau$) by the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability approximately balances the rate of viscous dissipation ($\epsilon$), thus setting up a quasi-stationary hydrodynamic turbulence. Then, the kinematic CHSI ensues.

Figure S2: The directions $x$ and $y$ are statistically homogeneous, whereas the shear-wise direction $z$ is statistically inhomogeneous. In this figure, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{t}$ denotes temporal (ensemble) average over the saturated stage of flow turbulence; thus, $\langle u_{i}\rangle_{t}$ denotes the time-average of the total flow $u_{i}$ in the system. The residual $\tilde{u}_{i}=u_{i}-\langle u_{i}\rangle_{t}$ features a full 3D spatial profile at each time. The symbol $\langle\tilde{u}_{i}\tilde{u}_{i}\rangle_{t}$ denotes the time-averaged 3D spatial profile of turbulent energy. From this quantity, inverse length scale $\Lambda_{i}$ of turbulence intensity is determined along each direction $i\in\{x,y,z\}$. Informed by this figure, mean is defined in simulations by averaging variables along the statistically homogeneous directions $x$ and $y$.

Figure S3: The spatial profiles of the Reynolds–Maxwell stress $R_{xz}$ are time-averaged over the CHSI phase ($t=200\textrm{--}1000$). The similarity between the profiles of $R_{xz}$ and $-\partial_{z}U_{x}$ indicates that turbulent momentum flux follows, to a good degree, the gradient-transport form in the simulation where the mean shear flow is maintained. This simulation with grid resolution of $512\times 512\times 1024$ is the same as the one shown in Fig. 1.

Figure S4: (a) The growth rate of turbulent cross helicity is measured in 3D MHD simulations by varying the time-scale $\tau_{\mathrm{f}}$ over which the mean shear flow is dynamically driven back to its initial unstable equilibrium. The parameter $\tau_{\rm f}=0$ represents the case where the mean shear flow is frozen in time. So long as the mean flow is maintained faster than it is depleted by the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability, the CHSI growth is observed. (b) The CHSI growth rate remains unchanged when the domain size $L_{y}/a\gg 1$ is further enlarged.

2610.28424.abstract: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

2610.28485.title: A Solar Optical Clock

The dispersed stellar spectrum is measured on a detector array, and Doppler shifts are determined by averaging the wavelength shifts of many lines across the stellar spectrum. (b) Schematic of a solar optical clock. A probe laser is locked to the center of a transition in the solar spectrum using heterodyne spectroscopy and modulation techniques. 2610.28485.abstract: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in $10^5$ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in $10^9$ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s$^{-1}$ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.

2610.28575.abstract: Small planets transiting the nearest M dwarfs are the terrestrial planets most accessible to detailed characterisation. We report a sub-Earth-sized transiting planet candidate in the wide (17.6") M-dwarf binary GJ 774 at 12.86 pc, most likely orbiting the M2.5 primary GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274). The signal was a SPOC multi-sector threshold-crossing event (MES = 7.95) and is not a TESS Object of Interest. In eight TESS sectors (2019-2026) a 1.28-h transit recurs every 4.225138 +/- 0.000010 d with a box-mean depth of 365 +/- 32 ppm in A's light. The 2026 data, which entered neither the SPOC search nor our selection, show it at the ephemeris predicted from 2019-2023 data (304 +/- 43 ppm; none of 10^5 phase-scrambled versions of the 2026 data is as deep). The per-target false-alarm probability is < 0.03 at 95%. Odd/even, secondary-eclipse, archival-plate and Gaia radial-velocity tests exclude unrelated blended eclipsing binaries and eclipsing companions on 4.2-d orbits, and hierarchical eclipsing binaries are improbable. The stars are 0.85 TESS pixel apart, so the TRICERATOPS false-positive probability (0.26) is set by a planet on GJ 774 B. B is disfavoured because its own light does not dim enough: PRF-deblended photometry gives 109 +/- 115 ppm in B's light, against 1089 ppm required if B were the host. Conditional on a point source at A or at B, the joint host model gives P(A)=0.59-0.97 (0.97 for the native target-pixel baseline). Over all sectors the PRF photometry is consistent with A, but in the out-of-sample 2026 data 40% of the deficit appears at B's position, an unexplained 2-3 sigma (PSF-model and depth dependent) tension with host A. On A the planet has R_p=0.70 +/- 0.06 R_Earth, S=15.0 +/- 1.8 S_Earth and T_eq=548 +/- 16 K. It is not validated; resolved ground-based photometry of the pair would test host B directly.
